messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Restrained): Feeling physically restrained or held down, Conflict: Confrontations, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Boonsong Rattanaporn is a 76-year-old Thai-American man who works part-time at a regional distribution warehouse on the outskirts of Sacramento, a job he took up in his early sixties and has held onto partly out of financial necessity and partly, he admits, because the physical routine of it gives his days a shape he can trust. He is unmarried, lives alone in a small apartment, and until recently had told no one — not a coworker, not a neighbor — about what he experienced as a young man in Southeast Asia during a period of intense civil conflict. He was in his early twenties when government forces swept through his village in rural Thailand during a period of counterinsurgency operations. Soldiers entered homes without warning. Boonsong was pulled from a back room, forced face-down onto the ground, and held there by two men — one with a knee pressed between his shoulder blades — while the air filled with the smell of burning thatch and diesel fuel from military vehicles idling in the lane outside. He remained pinned to the earth for what he estimates was close to an hour, unable to move, listening to shouting and the sounds of other villagers being questioned. He was eventually released without formal charges, but two men from his village were taken away and never returned. He left Thailand within the year, eventually making his way to the United States.

For decades, Boonsong managed. He worked, kept to himself, and did not speak of it. But in the years since his mid-sixties, and with increasing intensity over the past two, the memories have begun to find him in ways he cannot predict or prepare for. He describes them as vivid and complete — not fragments, but the full scene, with a clarity that disturbs him precisely because it feels more present than the room he is standing in. The smell of diesel exhaust from the loading dock vehicles at the warehouse, or the acrid trace of something burning in the break room microwave, can return him there instantly and without negotiation. He has stood frozen at the warehouse entrance on more than one occasion, unable to explain to younger coworkers why he has gone pale and still. When the memory returns in this way, the emotion that comes with it is so total that he has to sit down, sometimes on a pallet, sometimes on the floor, and wait for it to pass. He has missed portions of shifts this way. A supervisor, a man roughly half his age, noticed and asked Boonsong directly whether he was having health problems. Boonsong said it was his heart. It was easier than the truth.

Physical restraint remains one of the most potent experiences for him. During a routine stock-taking exercise several months ago, a younger coworker grabbed his arm from behind to stop him from stepping into the path of a forklift — a reasonable, even protective act. Boonsong's response was immediate and visceral: he wrenched away, his voice sharp, his body rigid. The coworker was startled and hurt. Boonsong apologized, but the interaction left him shaken for days. He had come to believe that something in him was broken in a way that could not be explained without sounding, as he put it to the intake clinician, "like a man who is not well in the mind." Confrontations of any kind — a raised voice in the warehouse, a dispute between coworkers, even a tense exchange on a television program — produce a state of vigilance in him that does not quickly resolve. He does not seek out arguments and goes to considerable lengths to avoid any situation that might escalate.

What finally brought Boonsong to the clinic was a conversation with a Vietnamese-American man at a community health fair who spoke openly about his own wartime experiences and the help he had received. Boonsong sat with that for three months before making an appointment. What he is most afraid of is being told that what happened to him does not qualify — that it was not bad enough, or too long ago to matter. What he is hoping for, stated quietly at the end of his intake session, is to be able to go to work without fearing what the air might carry in on any given morning.
